flashcards.q: What are the three things that cause a React component to re-render?
flashcards.a: Its own state changes (useState/useReducer), its parent re-renders and it isn't memoized, or a subscribed context value (useContext) changes. 'Props changed' is not independent -- it's a description of trigger #2.

flashcards.q: Why does index-as-key break a reorderable list's state?
flashcards.a: React matches list children by key. With index as key, the key at position 0 is always '0' regardless of which logical item is there after a reorder -- React reuses the DOM node/state at that position, silently reattaching it to the wrong logical item.

flashcards.q: Why must hooks be called unconditionally in the same order every render?
flashcards.a: React tracks each hook's state by its POSITION in a linked list attached to the fiber, not by name. A conditionally-skipped hook shifts every subsequent hook's slot, corrupting their stored state.

flashcards.q: Is the useEffect dependency array an optimization hint or a correctness contract?
flashcards.a: A correctness contract. Every reactive value read inside the effect that isn't in the array is a stale closure captured at the render that scheduled the effect, not read fresh when the effect runs.

flashcards.q: Why does React.memo sometimes have no effect even though it's applied correctly?
flashcards.a: memo does a shallow prop comparison. If a prop is a new object/array/function reference every render (an inline literal or unmemoized callback), the comparison always sees a difference even if contents are identical, so the component re-renders anyway.

flashcards.q: What is the systematic method for diagnosing 'why did this re-render'?
flashcards.a: React DevTools Profiler: record the interaction, use the 'why did this render' indicator to see the specific trigger, then fix at the source (reference instability, state location, context granularity) rather than reflexively wrapping in memo.

flashcards.q: Why is React's reconciliation O(n) instead of the general tree-diff O(n^3)?
flashcards.a: React makes two heuristic assumptions: elements of different types at the same position always produce different subtrees (remount rather than diff), and key is trusted as the developer-provided identity signal for list children, avoiding true minimal-edit-distance computation.

flashcards.q: What does the React Compiler do and since when has it been stable?
flashcards.a: Statically analyzes component code and automatically inserts memoization equivalent to manual useMemo/useCallback/React.memo. Stable 1.0 since October 2025, works back to React 17.

flashcards.q: Does the React Compiler eliminate the need to follow the Rules of Hooks?
flashcards.a: No -- the compiler depends on code following the Rules of Hooks and other React rules to safely analyze and transform it. Violations can cause a component to be silently skipped by the compiler, falling back to unoptimized behavior, not auto-fixed.

flashcards.q: Fix for a setInterval inside useEffect([]) that reads a stale count value via setCount(count+1)?
flashcards.a: Use the functional updater form: setCount(c => c+1). This avoids depending on the captured count entirely, so the effect can stay with empty deps without re-subscribing on every tick.

flashcards.q: Why does useLayoutEffect fix a visible flicker that useEffect causes when measuring and repositioning DOM elements?
flashcards.a: useEffect runs asynchronously AFTER the browser paints, so a layout-changing update inside it causes a visible pre-update paint then a corrected second paint. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM update but BEFORE paint, so the correction is reflected before anything is shown â€” one correct paint, no flicker.

flashcards.q: Why isn't useLayoutEffect the default over useEffect if it avoids flicker?
flashcards.a: It's synchronous and blocks the browser from painting until it completes, so using it for non-layout work (fetching, subscriptions, logging) adds unnecessary blocking to the critical rendering path. Reserve it specifically for synchronous DOM measurement-and-mutation that must be invisible to the user.
